clinicalPearls: Characteristically affects young women, often after a viral prodrome
Presents with acute, painless, unilateral visual loss with photopsia and a temporal or paracentral scotoma
Multiple small grey-white dots appear at the level of the outer retina and retinal pigment epithelium across the posterior pole and mid-periphery
A characteristic granularity of the fovea is a helpful diagnostic clue
An enlarged blind spot is frequently found on visual field testing
Fluorescein angiography shows a wreath-like pattern of hyperfluorescence and indocyanine green angiography shows hypofluorescent spots
The condition is self-limiting, so management is observation with recovery of vision over weeks
reference.pathophysiology: MEWDS is thought to represent a transient inflammatory disturbance of the photoreceptor and outer retinal complex together with the choriocapillaris, frequently following a viral illness. Disruption of the ellipsoid (photoreceptor) zone corresponds to the white dots and to the patient's visual symptoms. The process resolves spontaneously as the photoreceptor layer recovers, and vision returns to normal in most cases.
additionalDifferentials: Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination looking for the white dots and foveal granularity
Optical coherence tomography demonstrating ellipsoid zone disruption
Indocyanine green angiography showing hypofluorescent spots
Visual field testing to document an enlarged blind spot
redFlags: Bilateral or recurrent disease, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Progressive or persistent visual loss suggesting the acute zonal occult outer retinopathy spectrum
Features suggesting an infective cause such as syphilis
Profound loss that fails to recover
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; almost all patients recover good vision spontaneously over weeks to a few months, although mild residual symptoms occasionally persist.
pitfalls: Over-investigating or treating a self-limiting condition
Confusing it with other white-dot syndromes
Missing occasional recurrence or overlap with the acute zonal occult outer retinopathy spectrum
Failing to exclude syphilis in atypical cases
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course: Uveitis and Ocular Inflammation
management: Reassurance and observation, as the condition is self-limiting and vision recovers spontaneously in most patients over weeks to months
No specific pharmacological therapy is required, and corticosteroids are not routinely indicated given spontaneous resolution
Serial optical coherence tomography and fundus autofluorescence to document recovery of the ellipsoid (photoreceptor) zone
Visual field testing to monitor resolution of the enlarged blind spot and scotoma
Exclude alternative white-dot syndromes and infective or inflammatory mimics before settling on the diagnosis
Ophthalmology (retina) follow-up to confirm recovery and identify the rare recurrence or progression
